name: Senegal

facts.religion: Sunni Islam about 95%, mostly within Sufi brotherhoods

snapshot: The discovery of $13 billion in hidden debt froze an IMF programme and split the president from his own mentor, Prime Minister Ousmane Sonko.
culture: Senegal's Sufi brotherhoods, especially the Mourides, shape daily life, and the annual Grand Magal pilgrimage to Touba draws millions. Teranga, a Wolof word for hospitality, is a national value. Mbalax music, made famous by Youssou N'Dour, and laamb wrestling, with stars as famous as footballers, are national passions. Dakar hosts the Biennale of contemporary African art.
society: Senegal has never had a coup and has seen three peaceful transfers of power. Oil and gas production began in 2024. Fishing communities have been hit by foreign trawlers, and many young people attempt the dangerous Atlantic crossing to the Canary Islands. Wolof is the everyday language, French the official one.

story: In March 2024, Senegal did something rare: it put two men straight from prison into power. Ousmane Sonko was the opposition's star but was barred from running, so his protégé Bassirou Diomaye Faye ran instead on the slogan "Diomaye is Sonko," won, and made Sonko prime minister. Two years later the slogan is dead. On 22 May, Faye fired Sonko and dissolved the government (Reuters via Citizen Digital).

The break was about money. The new government discovered that its predecessor had hidden around $13 billion in debt, pushing the real figure to about 132 percent of GDP. The IMF froze a $1.8 billion programme. Faye wanted to negotiate with the Fund, possibly including a debt restructuring; Sonko called restructuring a "disgrace" and argued Senegal could raise taxes at home instead (Brookings). Behind the policy fight was a succession one: whether Faye would run again in 2029 or step aside for Sonko. Sonko did not disappear. By June he was speaker of the National Assembly, which his Pastef party dominates, and was installed as party leader at a rally in Dakar, and he later softened his line on IMF talks (bne IntelliNews). Senegal is now a president governing against the man who made him, with the legislature in his rival's hands, while it tries to dig out of a debt hole that will shape public spending for a decade.
briefing.power: A presidential republic. The president is directly elected for five years with a two-term limit and appoints the prime minister; the 165-seat National Assembly can censure the government. Senegal has never had a coup.
briefing.holders: President Bassirou Diomaye Faye; Ousmane Sonko controls the ruling party and the Assembly.
